rewrites.summary: Direction: mixed — the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America, with a repeating pattern of police round-ups of travestis and trans women in one neighbourhood. The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible scene and an LGBTQ-driven tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law alongside the national femicide registry — it is where state response is most likely to be present. For a trans visitor, the operative risk is police identification and detention: on 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women, writing several up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one — activists describe it as 'a new illegal procedure against travestis and trans', the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, making it a pattern rather than a single incident.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National-climate turbulence: 2025 set a record of at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity (+62% on 2024, one every 38 hours, the highest since monitoring began ten years ago), 32% of them inside police stations and penal facilities, with security-force violence multiplying from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis the majority of victims (142, 62.5%); federal closures of the equality ministry and the national anti-discrimination institute and dismissals of trans public-sector quota hires further erode recourse for visitors as for residents.
rewrites.localsOnly: Gender-marker rectification, the national employment quota for travesti/trans people (administered centrally from this city) and detention placement are resident-facing processes; visitors do not interact with them.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the police pattern in this neighbourhood persists as the activist accounts describe it is not independently verifiable from the audited sources. The national hate-crime and security-force counts carry no jurisdictional breakdown for the city, and the recourse erosion is documented at national level; the city's own machinery still operates, but its effective protection under the current national climate is not separately documented.

City-based activists told the outlet that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

A national-framework report: via emergency decrees published in February 2025, two decrees modified the gender-identity recognition law — one prohibited gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and the other re-regulated housing of transgender people deprived of liberty — inviting provinces and the capital city to adhere — prohibiting those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. Rights groups and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

rewrites.summary:
Direction: worse than national — the only Brazilian state in the country to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and the venue of a nationally decisive refusal. A trans woman was refused entry to the women's bathroom by staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre, urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to take public transport home; on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving these refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules — the legal exposure a visibly trans visitor faces using bathrooms in shops, restaurants and transport hubs.

In the other direction, the state has a visible LGBTQ tourism scene with pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages and marker changes, and nationwide legal rights are identical, so visitors see the same national protections as elsewhere.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Legislative flux: the bathroom restriction sits inside a continued escalation — a bill approved 22 December 2025 extending the ban to state and municipal public administration bodies, and a third bill tabled October 2025 that would restrict school and locker-room use to the sex recorded on the birth certificate. Nationally, a deeply conservative legislature has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the national court in 2013, while the national court separately ruled that nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity.
rewrites.localsOnly: School-bathroom rules, birth-certificate marker procedures and employment provisions are resident-facing; a visitor never enrols or works here.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General violent-crime exposure in this state mirrors the country's nationally leading lethality and is a risk to any resident or visitor regardless of gender identity; it does not move trans-specific risk.

Enforcement of the bathroom restriction in practice — who is challenged, where, and how often — is not documented, so actual exposure for visitors beyond the decided case is unverified; the third bill remains tabled and unenacted.

A law-firm guide for expats, updated April 2026: names the state/province's principal city among the country's broadly welcoming major cities with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name and gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories (spousal residence permit), foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes, joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed (2015 ruling), gender-marker changes proceed without surgery, and the 2019 ruling criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under a 1989 law.

rewrites.summary:
Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans killings. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a 32-year-old trans woman, Sara Millerey González Borja, was beaten and thrown into a waterway while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries. She was the third LGBT person killed in Bello that year — the first two were gay men — and the case triggered vigils, protests in several cities and a presidential order to investigate.

For a trans visitor the operative risk is lethal violence concentrated in this department's metro area: the surviving record supports a lethal concentration — three municipal killings within four months — and documents no department-level protection machinery specific to it.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National frame around that series, as documented: more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups in at least one southern department have circulated flyers announcing 'social cleansing' against trans women, in areas where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement; and a national tally recorded 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.
rewrites.localsOnly: No department-specific resident data is recorded: no cultural-role, birth-register or resident-discrimination fact for this department appears in the record.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No department-level protection machinery specific to this department is documented, and that absence is not evidence of safety. The investigation ordered after the April 2025 killing is not documented as concluded, and the national tallies above carry no departmental breakdown.

rewrites.summary:
Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Madrid (Chueca) ranks among the most visible LGBT urban scenes in Europe, with total anonymity in daily life; its Pride is among the largest in Europe. The national framework a visitor's documents stand under is the self-ID law of 28 February 2023: legal gender recognition from age 16 with no diagnosis required, with broad anti-discrimination guarantees and employment and health measures.

This community's own legislative divergence is statutory but narrow: on 27 December 2023 two community laws — Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023 — amended its 2016 gender-identity law and its anti-LGBTBI law on the stated ground of protecting freedom of expression and academic freedom, stripping the provisions that obliged educational institutions; the resulting restrictions sit in the school environment and do not touch a visitor's public conduct, documents or entry.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National and regional policy flux: this community was among the first to pass its own gender-identity law in 2016, and the 2023 amendments then narrowed that law and the community's anti-LGBTBI law; the national self-ID law of 28 February 2023 — hailed by a rights organisation as a hard-won victory for gender recognition, and backed by a national framework of discrimination and hate-crime provisions — remains in force beside the regional statutes, and their interaction has not been judicially tested.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: the 2023 community-level amendments that removed the 2016 trans-law obligations on educational institutions, and the 2022 education law's parental-primary-responsibility and school opt-out mechanism ('pin parental'), shape school environments for local families.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Evidentiary caveat: Madrid's citizens report LGTBI hate-crime offences to reporting services more than any other community's, so low recorded hostility here is not available as an alibi — the divergence is statutory, not statistical.

The record is a model estimate: the underlying best-knowledge delta and route-3 method are not independently verifiable, and no visitor documents, border-screening practice or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this community is recorded beyond the national provisions above.

It is the national framework that this state/province's 2023 amendments sit beside.
A rights organisation (February 2023) hails the parent nation's self-ID gender-recognition law as a hard-won victory for gender recognition after years of activism. National framework context.

A criminal-law firm analysis (June 2026): disentangles three statutes — what the 2023 equality law does and does not do; the discrimination aggravating factor of the penal code (gender identity and expression motives); and the hate offences extended to trans and LGBTI people. National framework context.

An encyclopaedic page on this state/province documents it as one of the main LGBT hubs and backs the record's route-3 claims about scene visibility: same-sex marriage legal since 2005, an annual Pride described as one of the largest in the country drawing millions of attendees, and a well-known central district as the epicentre of the community. It also records local institutions: a long-standing local LGBT organisation, a city diversity office, and a group focused on fighting discrimination and violence. Crucially for a traveller assessment, the article states that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems, and that marginalised LGBT groups, such as migrants and trans people, face additional barriers.

An encyclopaedic page on trans law is the national-framework document this state/province's record stands under: it records that this state/province was among the first regions to adopt its own gender-identity law, passing it in 2016 after an earlier region in 2015, which is the 2016 regional statute later amended; it also covers the national 2023 law on gender self-determination and the framework with which regional statutes must comply, giving the statutory floor a trans traveller stands under.
